title: Comparison items resist needing their texts
statement: Items comparing two texts are hard to make need the texts, since a comparison answer can often be guessed from the genres or a plausible particular.
example: In one course, multiple-choice comparison items keyed to how the two texts diverge leaked at blind-solve rates of 0.67 to 1.00.
detail: A Grade 7 reading course tried three constructions for its standard on comparing two texts, across a pair of accounts dense with particulars and a pair of poems making opposite claims. Multiple-choice items on how the texts diverge leaked at blind-solve rates of 0.67–1.00 because the genre schema is known in advance, claim-to-quote matching broke even with the passages, and a particular-anchored item that had certified another standard at 0.00 still leaked at 0.67. With no item under its dual-solver bar of blind-solve below 0.60, the course concluded that a comparison answer is either a schema-guessable interpretation or a semi-guessable plausible particular, and kept the standard taught and practised but ungated; that explanation is the course's own, drawn from the constructions it tried.
against: A Grade 8 course gated its two-text standard, which its course graph ties to comparing two arguments on one issue, with certified items in five formats: text entry 13, sequence 11, multiple choice 2, inline choice 3 and two-part 2 (`incept-package-hub/course-packages/courses/g8-reading/review/evidence/validation/coverage-matrix.json`, lines 46-52; `incept-package-hub/course-packages/courses/g8-reading/review/evidence/course-graph-guide.md`, line 28). It is a different demand from the Grade 7 standard, but it shows the limit may lie in the constructions tried rather than in comparison itself.
